newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian sugar industry braces for duty end.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian sugar industry braces for duty end.

text.p: Australia's A$300 million refined sugar market faces the prospect of stiffer competition when import tariffs are scrapped mid-year, producers and users said.
This was despite three years of price warfare which had cut local prices to less than world parity, they said.
Some producers fear European sugar will be dumped onto the Australian market, which consumes about 800,000 tonnes a year.
Others do not but concede that removal of the tariff could intensify competition for contracts with big industrial users.
Some contracts can be re-negotiated before expiry at year-end, while others will be re-negotiated for 1998.

"We don't have that fear that refined sugar would be dumped into Australia. One would doubt it -- dumped -- unlikely," Brian De Boos, general manager corporate affairs at leading sugar group, CSR Ltd, told Reuters.

The only way dumped sugar could enter Australia would be in packs because of the economics of transportation, and the retail market was minor compared with consumption by breweries, biscuit-makers and soft-drink manufacturers, he said.
Executives of other refiners, who asked that they not be named, said removal of the A$55 a tonne tariff on sugar imports was feared likely to encourage dumping.
Ending the tariff would also multiply the competitive levers available to big refined sugar users to extract even sweeter contract deals, they said.

Despite disagreement on the details, sugar producers and users contacted by Reuters agreed the July 1 scrapping of Australia's sugar import tariff would change the competitive balance in the industry.
"There's Aussie sugar in your Coke", said Ian Brown, general manager corporate affairs for Coca-Coca Amatil Ltd (CCA), Australia's largest industrial user of refined sugar.
The end of tariffs would not produce an immediate effect on where CCA drew its supplies from as the company held long-term contracts with Australian refiners, he said.
But Brown showed that CCA already plays a tough game in procuring refined sugar supplies. "We tend to buy our sugar fairly keenly, shall we say, as a fairly major user," he said.
Prices were not simple international parity plus freight but "part of a negotiating process."
CCA had economies of scale, could negotiate keenly and sellers' proposals would take that into account, he said.
CCA was well served by a competitive domestic market and was committed to long-term contracts, he also said.
CSR's De Boos sees the the power of big buyers possibly increased at year-end when new contracts are written. "(But it also) depends on how willing we are to lower prices even further," he said.
Australian raw sugar prices are already less than world parity, but removal of the tariff had the potential to spark dumping of refined product into Australia, one refiner said.
"Certainly a concern that we do have is what would happen if people starting just dumping refined sugar into Australia," he said, describing the world sugar market as "corrupt".
"It is a dumped market where everyone puts their residual production. That is what the sugar industry fears in the context of (loss of) tariff protection," he said.
European producers saw business sense in dumping sugar because, after charging high prices domestically, exports could cover marginal costs of production and attract rebates, he said.
Sugar refining executives said the industry was now concerned to see adequate government anti-dumping provisions.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
